title: India's Banks Are Offering NRIs Up to 7% on Dollar Deposits — and SBI's Leveraged Product Promises 11.25%
excerpt: The RBI's decision to absorb hedging costs on foreign currency deposits has triggered rate hikes of up to 310 basis points, could draw $35–40 billion in inflows, and is quietly reshaping how Indian banks fund themselves.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indian banks now offer up to 7.1% on FCNR deposits for NRIs.
  • RBI's hedging cost absorption has led to rate hikes of up to 310 basis points.
  • SBI's leveraged product allows returns up to 11.25% for qualifying deposits.
  • Expected inflows from this scheme could reach $35–40 billion.
  • The FCNR scheme aims to stabilize the rupee and boost foreign exchange reserves.

If you are an NRI with idle dollars sitting in a US savings account earning 4 per cent, Indian banks want your attention. Several of the country's largest lenders are now offering 6 to 7.1 per cent on Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) deposits, after the Reserve Bank of India's decision to absorb the full cost of hedging currency risk on these instruments — a move that has effectively tripled the returns banks can pass on to overseas depositors. ## How the RBI's Swap Subsidy Works The mechanics are straightforward but consequential. When an NRI parks dollars in an FCNR deposit, the receiving bank converts those dollars to rupees and lends them domestically. But the bank must return dollars when the deposit matures, which means it must hedge against rupee depreciation. That hedging — typically through sell-buy currency swaps — costs roughly 2.9 to 3.2 per cent annually, a burden that has historically capped the interest rate banks can offer NRIs at around 3.5 per cent. On June 5, 2026, the RBI announced it would bear the full hedging cost for three- to five-year FCNR(B) deposits raised through September 30. The effect was immediate. Within a week, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, and Bank of Baroda had raised their FCNR rates to a peak of 6 per cent — in some cases a jump of more than 300 basis points. ICICI and Axis hiked rates by 310 and 305 basis points respectively. Some smaller banks are offering as much as 7.1 per cent. ## SBI's 11.25 Per Cent Leveraged Product The State Bank of India went further. It launched a "leveraged FCNR(B) deposit product" under which a qualifying deposit of $100,000 can facilitate additional overseas borrowings of up to nine times the deposit amount, enabling investors to earn returns of up to 11.25 per cent over five years. The leveraging is conceptually unlimited, though it is constrained in practice by the availability of dollar funds with counterparty foreign banks and by the bank's own exposure limits. Other large banks including ICICI and HDFC are reportedly working on similar products. > **"SBI managing director Ashwini Kumar Tewari told CNBC-TV18 that the bank will go "all out" to market these schemes across West Asia, the United States, and Europe."** SBI managing director Ashwini Kumar Tewari told CNBC-TV18 that the bank will go "all out" to market these schemes across West Asia, the United States, and Europe. Punjab National Bank's CEO Ashok Chandra said PNB alone aims to raise $2.5 to $3 billion and expects the industry-wide take-up to reach $35 to $40 billion. ## Why Banks Are Scrambling for Dollars The enthusiasm is not just about NRI deposits. Indian banks have been fighting a structural funding problem. Credit growth has consistently outpaced deposit growth, and certificates of deposit (CDs) — a more expensive short-term funding tool — surged 38 per cent year-on-year in June, with banks raising ₹1.80 lakh crore through CDs in a single month. The RBI's FCNR scheme addresses this at multiple levels. First, it brings in longer-tenor, stable dollar deposits that reduce banks' dependence on expensive, short-dated CDs. Second, these deposits are exempt from cash reserve ratio (CRR) and statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) requirements, making them more capital-efficient. Third, the expected $60 to $70 billion in combined FCNR and external commercial borrowing inflows will boost systemic liquidity and push down funding costs more broadly. The results are already visible. The three-month CD reference rate fell to 6.65 per cent in late June from 7.25 per cent on June 4 — a plunge of 60 basis points in three weeks. Canara Bank's CEO said the measures will directly help net interest margins. Kotak Mutual Fund's head of fixed income expects CD rates to fall further, with the spread between three-month T-bills and CDs normalising from 140 basis points toward 100 basis points over the next quarter. ## What This Means for NRI Investors
Impact of RBI's Hedging Subsidy
›ICICI: 310 bps, Axis: 305 bps Rate hikes of up to 310 basis points.
›PNB aims for $2.5–3 billion Expected inflows of $35–40 billion.
›60 basis points drop Three-month CD rate fell to 6.65% from 7.25%.
›Longer-tenor dollar deposits reduce reliance on CDs.
For most NRIs, the straightforward play is a 3-to-5-year FCNR deposit earning 6 to 7 per cent with no currency risk on the dollar principal, since these deposits are denominated in foreign currency and repaid in the same currency. The interest earned is also tax-free in India for NRIs, and the deposit is insured up to ₹5 lakh under the DICGC scheme. The leveraged SBI product offers higher returns but carries proportionally higher risk: it involves borrowing against the deposit to deploy more capital, and any mismatch in timing or rates could erode the headline yield. Financial advisers suggest the leveraged route is best suited to sophisticated investors who understand the downside. The September 30 deadline for the RBI's hedging subsidy means the window is time-limited. Whether the central bank extends it will likely depend on the quantum of flows and the rupee's trajectory. Governor Sanjay Malhotra has said the RBI is "hopeful of reasonable flows" but is not targeting a specific amount. ## The Bigger Picture At a macro level, the FCNR scheme is the latest in a series of RBI moves to stabilise the rupee, which has weakened roughly 11 per cent against the dollar over the past year. By incentivising dollar inflows through the banking channel, the central bank is building foreign exchange reserves — which crossed $660 billion in April but have since dipped — without directly intervening in currency markets. For NRIs, it represents a rare alignment of incentives: better returns than US Treasuries, regulatory backing from the central bank, and a contribution to India's external stability. Whether the opportunity outlasts its September window remains to be seen. --- **Sources:** Reuters; Mint (LiveMint); The Hindu BusinessLine; Punjab National Bank CEO interview (Reuters, June 2026); RBI Monetary Policy Statement, June 5, 2026.
